edits.safety: Vault pages are private family data and belong on the two parents' own agents, which have no browse tool; the research agent that reads manuals holds none of it. The vault is one for the whole gateway. OpenClaw's page says to give each agent its own vault when agents must not share wiki pages (memory-wiki.md:59), and in that mode every agent gets a separate vault, so the two parents could not share one; with the shared vault the other agents are kept out by tool policy alone: the wiki tools go to the two mains only, and because the pages can also be reached through ordinary memory search where the memory engine supports it (memory-wiki.md:298), memory search stays off on the shared agents and the mail readers. Leave the plugin in its default `isolated` mode: as read on the same page (line 467) and not tried, bridge mode checks which agent owns an imported memory note only for per-agent vaults, so on the shared vault it could compile each parent's own notes (F041) into the handbook. A data-plate photo is untrusted content read by an agent with memory; that agent has no browser or fetch tool, and the ways out the roadmap lists for it are a text to its owner (or, once family delivery exists, the family) and the task text it hands to the research helper, which the roadmap names as the one remaining leak path. Once step 2 lets an agent write pages, the handbook is also a place where an instruction hidden in a photo, a document or a research result could persist, and because the vault is shared the other parent's agent reads it back too; the agent is told to save a page only when a parent asks (an instruction, not an enforced limit), and the weekly review (G006) as written today lists memory-file saves and in-house tool writes but not `wiki_apply` pages, so vault saves need a row there when step 2 is built.

demand_source.title: Connect the Google Workspace app to Gemini Apps - Gemini Apps Help
demand_source.supports: Google's own assistant offers consumers summaries and quick answers drawn from their Gmail, the same read-only lookup this gives each adult's mail agent; opened again in this round.

caveats: The roadmap's M4 keeps each inbox on a local model and none is installed, so the lookup and the digest both send personal mail to the cloud model, and without Zero Data Retention the 30-day abuse-monitoring log applies to that text; this is Tony's open decision and the whole card waits on it.

Waiting for a local model is not the safer choice on every count. OpenClaw's security page says not to use older, weaker or smaller model tiers for untrusted inboxes or for agents that hold tools (gateway/security/prompt-injection.md:47). The roadmap's local-model milestone says no local model gets tools that touch untrusted content, while its mail milestone allows the reader one read-only mail tool if the Gmail route is chosen, and the lookup cannot work without that search tool. So the decision trades privacy (mail text stays on the Mac) against resistance to a mail written to mislead (the stronger cloud model).

Google already does much of this where the mail lives: the Gemini app answers questions from a person's own Gmail and lists a daily digest of calendar, to-dos and emails among its scheduled actions, and Gmail's 'AI Inbox' was announced in January 2026, so try those on one parent's account before building; Happy adds only asking, and being told, in the iMessage thread.

-main` always loses `message` and `session_status`; that a before_tool_call hook reaches MCP tool calls is implied by the docs but not stated.
'Memory off' is not one switch: memory search has a per-agent override, dreaming is plugin-wide, and the session-exclusion setting only matches hook sessions.

Reply drafts are left out, 'subject line only for health senders' and 'do not open the form' are instructions to the agent and not enforced limits, and the tax-form check only knows that a notice email arrived, so a form that came by post or sits in a portal shows as missing.

The lookup goes one step beyond the roadmap's design, where a mail agent's only output is its scheduled text to the owner: here the answer comes back into the parent's own agent, which holds that parent's notes and may hand a task to the research helper (F019). OpenClaw's security page recommends the first half of this shape (a read-only reader agent summarises untrusted content and passes the summary to the main agent, gateway/security/prompt-injection.md:34) and warns about the second: deny `sessions_spawn` to an agent that handles untrusted content (gateway/security/tool-permissions.md:21), and the parent's agent keeps that tool for the research hand-off, which the roadmap already names as its one remaining leak path. So the lookup needs its own test with a seeded misleading mail, or the card can start with the digest alone.

edits.description: 'Email me this': long answers, tables and plans land in the asker's own inbox, as plain text in the first version, from a dedicated family sender. A hook that fails closed is meant to block any send that is not addressed to the asker alone; that block has to be proven with test sends before go-live.
edits.example: Jordan texts: 'Email me the camp comparison.' The full comparison arrives in her own inbox as plain text from the family sender address. A send with anyone else on the To, cc or bcc line, or one sent as a reply-all, is meant to be blocked by the hook, and that block is tested before go-live.
edits.how:
A send-only mail tool on a dedicated family sender account: the gog MCP server with the write flag plus its separate `--allow-gmail-send` flag and only `gmail_send_message` allowed, granted to `

-main` only. A `before_tool_call` hook blocks the call unless the recipient equals the owner address of the calling agent and cc and bcc are empty; it also blocks any call that carries reply context or a reply-all target (upstream says a send needs 'recipients or a reply-all target', so a reply-all could reach other people with no recipient field at all), a send-as alias, or an HTML body (`body_html`), so mail goes out as plain text. A block is terminal and the hook fails closed. Do not rely on rewriting the recipient: the docs describe rewrites for host-owned tool parameters only. An in-house daily send cap. Sign the sender account in with a send-only grant if the installed gog supports it (the upstream command reference lists a `send` mode for `--gmail-scope` on `gog auth add`), so that the token cannot read that mailbox.
caveats: The promise that nobody else can be a recipient rests on an in-house hook, and it is not yet shown that the hook sees every field that can set a recipient: to, cc and bcc, and also the reply fields, because the upstream page for the mail tool says a send needs 'recipients or a reply-all target', so a reply-all could address other people with no recipient listed. A seeded send to a non-owner address and a seeded reply-all must both be blocked before this goes live.
The hook blocks a wrong recipient; it does not correct it, because the docs describe rewriting parameters for host-owned tools only.

Pinning the recipient does not close every way out. The mailed text is often built from research results, and a link in it, or a remote image in an HTML mail, can carry private text in its address to whoever runs that site once the link is clicked or the mail is opened (the 'lethal trifecta' post the roadmap takes its rule from names loading an image and offering a link to click as ways data gets out). The upstream tool accepts an HTML body, so the hook refuses it and the first version sends plain text only; a link in the text is still only as trustworthy as the result it came from.
Plain text means a table arrives as lined-up text, not as a formatted table; an HTML body is a later choice and would need the hook to refuse remote images.
It needs a dedicated family sender Google account with a send grant, set up by hand outside OpenClaw, and a daily send cap that is in-house code (no built-in cap was found).
gog's quickstart says a Google sign-in app left in Testing issues tokens that expire after seven days, so the sender account needs the app published to In production, as the mail reader (G015) does.
unverified: That the hook sees every field of the gog MCP send tool that can set a recipient: the upstream MCP page names recipients, reply context, a reply-all target and send-as aliases as inputs but does not list the tool's input schema, so whether cc and bcc are separate fields is not known. Read the schema from the installed server and prove the block with a seeded send to a non-owner address and a seeded reply-all.
A daily send cap is in-house code; no built-in cap was found in the pages read.
Creating the dedicated family sender account and granting its send scope is a manual step outside OpenClaw.

That `gog auth add --gmail-scope send` exists on the installed version and that the MCP send tool works under a send-only grant: the flag was read in the upstream command reference, and gog is not installed on this Mac.
edits.safety: The send tool sits on each parent's own agent, which holds private data, so the recipient pin is the protection: a fail-closed hook blocks any send that is not addressed to the calling agent's owner alone, with no cc or bcc, no reply or reply-all target and no send-as alias, and the tool is granted to no shared or mail-reading agent. Mail leaves from a dedicated family sender address, not from a parent's own account, and as plain text, so it cannot carry a remote image that reports back when the mail is opened; a link in the text can still do that if it is clicked.

gog installed on the Mac mini
